'''''Amaranthus hypochondriacus''''' is an [[ornamental plant]] commonly known as '''Prince-of-Wales feather'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=AMHY2|taxon=Amaranthus hypochondriacus|accessdate=7 January 2016}}</ref> or '''prince's-feather'''.<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | author=Phillips, Edward | title=The New World of Words. ''7th ed'' | year=1720 | authorlink=Edward Phillips| title-link=The New World of English Words }}</ref> It is called ''quelite, bledo''<ref name=RLC>{{cite web |url=http://www.rlc.fao.org/es/agricultura/produ/cdrom/contenido/libro11/cap4.htm |title=''Cultivos andinos: Introducción'' |accessdate=2011-02-04 |work=[[FAO]]: Oficina Regional de para América Latina y el Caribe |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110110075046/http://www.rlc.fao.org/es/agricultura/produ/cdrom/contenido/libro11/cap4.htm |archive-date=2011-01-10 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and ''quintonil'' in Spanish.<ref name=UNAM>{{cite web |url=http://www.ibiologia.unam.mx/herbario/galerias/colecciones_asociadas/pages/Semillas_amaranto.html |title=''Semillas de Amaranto'' |accessdate=2011-02-04 |work=[[UNAM]]: Colección Etnobotánica |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722231127/http://www.ibiologia.unam.mx/herbario/galerias/colecciones_asociadas/pages/Semillas_amaranto.html |archive-date=2011-07-22 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=UDG>{{cite web |url=http://www.cucba.udg.mx/sitiosinteres/coaxican/plts_mex/amaranto/amaranto.htm |title=''El amaranto'' |accessdate=2011-02-04 |work=[[University of Guadalajara]]: Centro Universitario de Biológicas y Afropecuarias |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110102153342/http://www.cucba.udg.mx/sitiosinteres/coaxican/plts_mex/amaranto/amaranto.htm |archive-date=2011-01-02 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Description ==
''A. hypochondriacus'' is a vigorous, upright plant that typically reaches {{convert|40-200|cm|in|round=5|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Amaranthus hypochondriacus - Useful Tropical Plants|url=http://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Amaranthus+hypochondriacus|access-date=2021-05-06|website=tropical.theferns.info}}</ref> It is often grown for its [[flower]]s, which appear in dense, catkin-like [[inflorescence]]s in the summer and autumn. They are usually deep purplish-red, but may be yellow-green.<ref name=":1" /> These give way to dry [[fruit]]s, about {{convert|1.5-3|mm|in|frac=32|abbr=on}} long, that split open when ripe.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Amaranthus hypochondriacus (prince's-feather amaranth): Go Botany |url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/amaranthus/hypochondriacus/ |access-date=2021-05-06 |website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org}}</ref> The fruits contain smooth, shiny seeds that may be [[subglobose]] to [[Lenticular (botany)|lenticular]], either whitish-pink or dark reddish-brown to black, and {{convert|1-1.4|mm|in|frac=64|abbr=in}} in diameter.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Amaranthus hypochondriacus in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200006983 |access-date=2021-05-06 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref> The leaves are simple and alternately arranged, with entire margins.<ref name=":2" /> They are rhombic-ovate to broadly [[lanceolate]] in shape, about {{convert|4-12|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=in}} long and {{convert|2-7|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=in}} wide, borne on long [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]].<ref name=":3" />

== Taxonomy ==
Originally endemic to [[Mexico]],{{Additional citation needed|date=February 2026}} there is near certainty that ''A. hypochondriacus'' is the common ancestor to the genus ''[[Amaranthus]]'', but the later domestication of groups remains unclear. There has been opposing hypotheses of a single as opposed to multiple domestication events of the three grain species.<ref name="stetter1">{{Cite journal |last1=Stetter |first1=Markus G. |last2=Schmid |first2=Karl J |date=April 2017 |title=Analysis of phylogenetic relationships and genome size evolution of the ''Amaranthus'' genus using GBS indicates the ancestors of an ancient crop |journal=Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution |volume=109 |pages=80–92 |bibcode=2017MolPE.109...80S |doi=10.1016/j.ympev.2016.12.029 |pmid=28057554 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="joshi">{{Cite journal |last1=Joshi |first1=Dinesh C. |last2=Sood |first2=Salej |last3=Hosahatti |first3=Rajashekara |last4=Kant |first4=Lakshmi |last5=Pattanayak |first5=A. |last6=Kumar |first6=Anil |last7=Yadav |first7=Dinesh |last8=Stetter |first8=Markus G. |date=2018-07-10 |title=From zero to hero: the past, present and future of grain amaranth breeding |journal=Theoretical and Applied Genetics |volume=131 |issue=9 |pages=1807–1823 |doi=10.1007/s00122-018-3138-y |issn=0040-5752 |pmid=29992369 |s2cid=49669284}}</ref> There is evidence of phylogenetic and geographical support for clear groupings that indicate separate domestication events in South America and Central America.<ref name="stetter1" /> ''[[Amaranthus hybridus|A. hybridus]]'' may derive from South America, whereas ''[[Amaranthus caudatus|A. caudatus]]'', ''A. hypochondriacus'', and ''[[Amaranthus quentiensis|A. quentiensis]]'' are native to Central America and elsewhere in North America.<ref name="stetter1" /><ref name="joshi" />

== Uses ==
In [[temperate]] regions, it is cultivated as a [[hardiness (plants)|half-hardy]] [[annual plant]]. Numerous [[cultivars]] have been selected, of which 'Green Thumb'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/106045/Amaranthus-hypochondriacus-Green-Thumb/Details | title = ''Amaranthus hypochondriacus'' 'Green Thumb' | publisher = RHS | accessdate = 19 March 2020}}</ref> and 'Pygmy Torch'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/106046/Amaranthus-hypochondriacus-Pygmy-Torch/Details | title = ''Amaranthus hypochondriacus'' 'Pygmy Torch' | publisher = RHS | accessdate = 19 March 2020}}</ref>  have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]. It grows best in well-drained soils in full sun, and is suitable for [[Hardiness zone|USDA hardiness zones]] 3–10. It may be susceptible to [[aphid]]s.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Amaranthus hypochondriacus (Cocks Comb, Lady Bleeding, Love Lies Bleeding, Pile Wort, Prince-of-Wales Feather, Prince's Feather, Prince's-feather, Red Cocks Comb) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/amaranthus-hypochondriacus/|access-date=2021-05-06|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref>

In [[Africa]] and [[El Salvador]], like many other species in the family [[Amaranthaceae]], it is valued as source of food.<ref name="prota">Grubben, G.J.H. & Denton, O.A. (2004) Plant Resources of Tropical Africa 2. Vegetables. PROTA Foundation, Wageningen; Backhuys, Leiden; CTA, Wageningen.</ref> The [[Leaf|leaves]] and [[seed]]s are very nutritious and have a mild flavor.<ref name=":0" /> The seeds also contain [[Phenols|phenolic compounds]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barba de la Rosa |first1=A.P. |last2=Fomsgaard |first2=Inge S. |last3=Laursen |first3=Bente |last4=Mortensen |first4=Anne G. |last5=Olvera-Martínez |first5=L. |last6=Silva-Sánchez |first6=C. |last7=Mendoza-Herrera |first7=A. |last8=González-Castañeda |first8=J. |last9=De León-Rodríguez |first9=A. |date=2009-01-01 |title=Amaranth (Amaranthus hypochondriacus) as an alternative crop for sustainable food production: Phenolic acids and flavonoids with potential impact on its nutraceutical quality |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0733521008001355 |journal=Journal of Cereal Science |language=en |volume=49 |issue=1 |pages=117–121 |doi=10.1016/j.jcs.2008.07.012 |issn=0733-5210 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>
